correctness.rationale: For every finite graph \(H\), the old vertices \(X\) selected by an independent dominating set of \(\mathtt C(H)\) form a clique, and subdivision choices are forced to correspond exactly to \(E(H-X)\). The sole possible domination obstruction is \(N_H(v)=X\) for an old vertex \(v\notin X\). When \(H=\mathtt C(G)\), every subdivision-vertex neighborhood is a nonedge pair and every old-vertex neighborhood contains an isolated subdivision vertex and has size at least two, so no open neighborhood is a clique. Thus every clique gives a unique independent dominating set. Cliques in \(\mathtt C(G)\) consist exhaustively of independent old-vertex subsets, singleton subdivision vertices, and incident old-subdivision pairs. Their multiplicities are respectively \(a_s(G)\), \(m\), and \(2m\), and their sizes are respectively \(e_s\), \(M-1\), and \(M-n+2\), giving the full polynomial. The optimizer classification follows from \(e_{s+1}-e_s=s+2-n\), with complete-graph and star boundaries separately handled. A separate standard-library verifier independently enumerated all maximal independent sets in the double central graph for all \(770\) connected labelled hosts through five vertices and \(100\) seeded six-vertex hosts, finding agreement for \(21{,}149\) independent dominating sets. The bounded enumeration is not treated as a proof of the infinite theorem.

value.rationale: The universal polynomial transfer is the natural exact enumerative counterpart of the recent central-graph independent-domination problem. It computes the entire independent-domination cardinality profile of the second iterate from the ordinary independence polynomial of any connected input, rather than merely giving an extremal scalar. The total-count identity \(|\mathcal{ID}(\mathtt C^2(G))|=\sum_s a_s(G)+3m\) holds for every connected input of order at least three. The minimum-set correspondence singles out precisely two motivated exceptions, complete graphs and stars; except for stars, the output degree profile recovers the original independence polynomial. This explains structurally why a natural graph operation preserves enumerative information and addresses a general graph-invariant transformation rather than an arbitrary small case.
